summary:
Earth System Trend Detective is a web app that checks whether a climate trend at any place on Earth is real or just noise. Users pick a location by preset, search or coordinates, then choose one of 18 NASA POWER variables, such as temperature, frost days, rainfall, humidity, solar radiation or aerosol haze, plus a season and a year range from 1981 onward.

The app runs a Mann–Kendall test for significance and uses Sen's slope to estimate the rate of change. It also compares the change with normal year-to-year variability. A map tab repeats the test across nearby grid cells to show whether the signal is local or regional, and an optional extension shows where the trend would lead by 2035 or 2050.

Built-in cases, such as Arctic autumn nights warming about 2 °C per decade, make it easy to start. Any view can be shared with a link!
details:
What it does: Earth System Trend Detective tests whether a climate trend at a place is real or just noise. Users choose a place (preset, name search or coordinates), one of 18 NASA POWER variables (temperature, frost days, precipitation, humidity, wind, solar radiation, cloud cover, aerosol optical depth), a season and a year range from 1981 onward.

How it works: The app pulls monthly data from the NASA POWER API and builds a seasonal series. It runs a Mann–Kendall test for significance and uses Sen's slope to estimate the rate of change. It also compares the total change with normal year-to-year variability (signal/noise). A map tab runs the same test on nearby grid cells to show whether a change is local or regional. Other tabs show monthly anomalies, an illustrative extension of the trend to 2035 or 2050 with a clear "not a forecast" note, and a CSV download.

Benefits and impact: Students, journalists and local planners can check a claim like "our winters are getting warmer" in a few clicks, with an honest p-value instead of a guess. Built-in cases, such as Arctic autumn nights warming about 2 °C per decade with p < 0.001, show how to read the results. Any view can be shared with a link.

Tools: Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Plotly and the NASA POWER API. The app is deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud, and the code is on GitHub with automated tests.

What we considered: The app avoids overclaiming: it states that significance does not prove cause, that extensions are not forecasts, and that map p-values are not adjusted for multiple comparisons. It also shows the record start date for each variable.

See the full app: https://earth-trend-detective-encxzet2yvnrtkcnsuwa6j.streamlit.app/
